title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Talk at TiE SoCal in Irvine, on Marketing & Branding on Feb 24, 2014
summary: Pabrai tells a room of entrepreneurs that marketing is an exact science with laws (Davidow, Miller-Heiman): segment to win 50-60% share, never pitch something you wouldn't buy, keep the message truthful because customers' subconscious detects lies, and listen closely to customer feedback in the early days. He explains why strong marketing lets a weak sales engine work (he raised ~$150 million in six weeks without leaving Irvine), why cloning is his core business practice (Pabrai Funds cloned the Buffett Partnership; now buying an insurance company like Berkshire), and closes with Buffett's inner scorecard and the 'bowl with bumpers' cloning approach to stock picking.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurship is what makes the wheel turn; Munger says Costco has done more good for the world than the Rockefeller Foundation.
ideas.detail: Jobs, growth and social good all start with an entrepreneur dreaming an impossible dream, which is why he respects TiE's mission.

ideas.idea: Marketing is an exact science with laws like physics; ignore them and, like gravity, they will still bite you.
ideas.detail: He learned this in the mid-1980s from William Davidow's Marketing High Technology (Davidow ran R&D then marketing at Intel) and the Miller-Heiman books Strategic Selling, Conceptual Selling and Successful Large Account Management; 90-95% of entrepreneurs don't know the rules and predictably hit a brick wall.

ideas.idea: In any market three or four players control 80%, so if your plan is to take 2-10% of a market you have not segmented it properly; don't start unless you have a clear plan to win 50-60% share.
ideas.detail: Inverting Davidow's law, as Munger advises, the '$10 billion market, I just need 10%' pitch is a fatal flaw; either the segmentation is wrong or the offering isn't compelling.

ideas.idea: The stronger the marketing, the weaker the sales engine can be; do the marketing homework and even a leper can make sales.
ideas.detail: He considers himself a poor salesman and a strong marketer; skimping on marketing means spending 50x the time banging your head on the sales end. He raised ~$150 million in about six weeks for an insurance company purchase without leaving Irvine and it oversubscribed.

ideas.idea: Don't try to sell something you wouldn't buy yourself, and never put lipstick on a pig, because customers' subconscious sees through lies.
ideas.detail: From Munger's rule and David Hawkins' Power vs. Force: a lie is detected subconsciously even if not consciously, which is why P&G will never market a claim that isn't true and a genuine improvement, and why 40,000 people flock to Omaha for Buffett's truthful 'attractor field'.

ideas.idea: Your initial idea is probably 10-70% right, so in the early days pay close attention to customer feedback; what works is usually a tangent, not what you came up with.
ideas.detail: InstallShield's founder Viresh pitched seven tools at a trade show and the eighth afterthought bullet, a software installer that didn't yet exist, was the one lead that became the company. Pabrai noticed 50% of his new fund's investors were Indians (2% of the US population), a signal a good marketer would hone the next message around.

ideas.idea: Most Inc. 500 entrepreneurs started as arbitrage players with non-enduring advantages, staying a few months ahead of competitors until they found something scalable.
ideas.detail: Amar Bhide's The Origin and Evolution of New Businesses documents this; the CompuLink founder made non-standard cable lengths on consignment for Florida computer stores, earned supernormal profits for months until branded makers caught up, kept hopping ahead, and eventually built an 1,800-person cable installation services business.

ideas.idea: Make your startup look larger: I carried a 'Vice President Marketing' card at TransTech rather than 'President and CEO' when pitching Fortune 500 clients, and Bhide found half of successful founders did the same.
ideas.detail: Founders independently added 'international' or 'global' to company names; reading the book's list of what worked lets a new entrepreneur incorporate proven tactics.

ideas.idea: Tom Peters was right: you can lay out all your trade secrets to competitors and they will not change their behavior, which is why cloning is so powerful and so rare.
ideas.detail: Peters' story of the self-serve gas station owner who gave random free full-service and took business from a rival who never adapted; Pabrai tested it by explaining everything to employees leaving TransTech to compete with him, and not one followed any of it.

ideas.idea: Cloning is an exercise in humility, admitting everyone else is smarter than you, and my entire livelihood is based on it: Pabrai Funds was cloned from the Buffett Partnerships.
ideas.detail: From 1969 when Buffett closed his partnership to 1999 nobody had cloned the most successful hedge fund model in history, so he did and his family's net worth is significantly higher for it; he is now buying an insurance company because that is the Berkshire Hathaway model.

ideas.idea: Build competitive advantage one tiny cloned best practice at a time; small things like a law firm's elegant mailing label or a $400 Caliper personality test before every hire add up to something meaningful.
ideas.detail: He never hires even interns without the Caliper test, including a 15,000-rupee-a-month Dakshana alum where the test is 50% of the wage, because bad hires are among the most expensive things that can happen to a company; the CEOs he tells rarely adopt it because the cloning gene is missing.

ideas.idea: Build a brand for infrequent big-ticket relationships the way Multani Jewelers did with a one-rupee Diwali card every year for 20 years; I clone it with physical family-photo greeting cards.
ideas.detail: Humans love looking at other humans (Facebook users look most at their own pictures), so a family picture card beats a Christmas tree card; as everyone moves online, his use of the US Postal Service keeps rising because physical cards now stand out more.

ideas.idea: Cialdini's reciprocation bias is uncalibrated, so a $50 Cross pen mailed with every Pabrai Funds package creates goodwill and obligation that can be repaid with a million-dollar wire.
ideas.detail: Like the Moonies' airport flower but with a 100% acceptance rate; fewer than 1 in 200 return the pen, and even non-investors feel good about him. Humans evolved to store meat in neighbors' bellies and remember favors without calibrating their size.

ideas.idea: Live sales meetings are incredibly expensive in time and money; build a back end strong enough that you can do things the Amazon way with no phone number.
ideas.detail: A local meeting blows half a day and an out-of-town one costs $1,000-plus and a day or two; during his $150 million raise he visited only one investor, in Irvine, and did the rest by phone. If the marketing message isn't buttoned down the live meeting won't be fruitful anyway.

ideas.idea: Cloners are not doomed to trail: Microsoft, Walmart and Pepsi are clone businesses, and when you clone you add your own nuance, which becomes the advantage.
ideas.detail: Word cloned WordPerfect, Excel cloned Lotus, Bing clones Google, and Microsoft needs 5-7 versions to get it right yet built a great business; Sam Walton copied Sears for 20 years with no new ideas except small towns and extreme cost discipline (four to a hotel room, coach only). Pabrai Funds cloned Buffett but is different when you drill down.

ideas.idea: Live by an inner scorecard, not an outer one: do what you believe is right regardless of whether the world agrees.
ideas.detail: At his 2008 charity lunch, which he treated as gurudakshana to thank Buffett for all the cloning, Buffett's first point was the inner scorecard: would you rather be the best lover in the world but known as the worst, or the reverse? Buffett doesn't care what the world thinks, as his unconventional personal arrangements showed.

ideas.idea: Talking to another human is the least efficient way to pick up data; reading is the densest way to educate yourself and catch market signals.
ideas.detail: Spend maximum time with customers in the early days, but afterwards be a voracious reader rather than a voracious meeter of people, because meetings are mostly banter with little essence.

ideas.idea: There are 100 ways to succeed: Steve Jobs waited for perfection and Bill Gates shipped half-baked, and both worked; my bias is to ship something you love and would use yourself.
ideas.detail: Advice to a founder with a patented whitening gel: it's a gut call, call the next iteration version 2.0 after a year, but if you have reservations keep it in the lab longer.

ideas.idea: Match investing approach to ability: an 80 IQ should dollar-cost-average into the S&P 500, a 90 IQ into Berkshire Hathaway, and a 100 IQ can simply copy Buffett's disclosed trades.
ideas.detail: A 30-year study (1976-2006) by professors at Ohio State and Nevada found that buying Buffett's picks at the month-end high after public disclosure and selling at the month-end low when he sold returned 21.5% annualized, beating the S&P by 11.5 points a year, with 15 minutes of work a month. Beating the index by 3 points makes you one in 200.

ideas.idea: Always bowl with bumpers: almost my entire portfolio is stock picks cloned from other great investors, and I have no original ideas.
ideas.detail: What matters is the score, not whether you used bumpers; he looks at what a smart investor did, checks whether he understands it, buys the same thing and gets paid for it. He notes a new cloning ETF had just launched.

ideas.idea: Owning Berkshire Hathaway is a great, simple choice with no taxes until you sell; I hold one share now but have held significant amounts when it was cheaper.
ideas.detail: He keeps one share to stay eligible for the annual meeting and buys more when it gets cheap.
